headline: Southwest Ledge Turned Green and Cold Overnight — Bass Sliding Deep, Bonito Watch Stays Hot
subhead: A temperature break off the Ledge has the bass program shifting nocturnal while the island keeps one eye on the horizon for the season's first false albacore.
body_markdown:
I felt it before I saw it. Ran out to the Southwest Ledge Tuesday morning before first light and the air had that different weight to it — heavier, cooler, the kind of morning that tells you the water underneath has shifted even if the surface looks the same. Sure enough, when I dropped the temp gauge over the side, we'd dropped a couple degrees from where we sat a week ago. That's the whole story right there. The warm surface mass that's been sitting on the Sound and pushing up from the Jersey coast has finally started interacting with the cold, clean upwelling that makes this island what it is, and the bass know it before we do.

Here's the thing about Block Island in late July — when the surface water gets into the mid-70s and pushes toward 80 like it has the last two weeks, the bass don't leave, they just go down and go quiet during the day. I've fished this pattern every summer for twenty-some years and it never fails. The fish stack on the deeper structure — the Ledge itself, the drop-off on the north side of the North Rip, the humps off Coast Guard Channel — and they wait for the tide change or full dark to feed. We caught bass to 34 pounds this week, but every single one of them came between 9pm and 3am, on the last two hours of the ebb into the start of the flood, over 35 to 55 feet of water on the Ledge. Bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig, 3-ounce egg sinker, 40-pound fluorocarbon leader, is still the most reliable way to connect after dark. If you want to go artificial, a 9-inch black or dark green Slug-Go worked slow along the bottom on the drift has been drawing strikes too — the darker profile shows up better against a night sky than anything bright.

Daytime striper fishing has been tougher, and I'm not going to sugarcoat it. We worked the North Rip hard on Thursday afternoon during a strong tide change and only picked at fish — three keepers in four hours of drifting live eels through the rip, which on a good July day should produce a lot more than that. The water up top is just too warm for them to commit during daylight right now. If you're set on a day trip, fish the last hour of daylight into dusk on the west side of the island off Grace's Cove, where the bottom holds cooler water longer, or hit the rips right at the tide change and don't waste time on slack water — the bass simply aren't using the structure when the current stops moving.

Bluefish have been the daytime save. They don't care about the warm water the way stripers do, and we've had steady action on choppers from 4 to 9 pounds working peanut bunker schools off the south side of the island, particularly around Black Rock and down toward Southeast Light. Bucktails in white or chartreuse, half-ounce to an ounce depending on how deep the bait's holding, fished on a fast retrieve through the bait balls, will get bit almost every cast when the birds are working. It's not subtle fishing but it's produced when the bass wouldn't.

Fluke have been the most dependable meat-in-the-cooler fish this week. Drifting the sand and gravel patches off Charlestown Beach and the entrance to Great Salt Pond, 20 to 35 feet, we've had keepers to 6 pounds on the outgoing tide using a classic Fluke Killer rig — a white bucktail teaser ahead of a 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a 3/4-ounce jig head, dragged just off bottom. It's a steady program, not a blitz, but you'll put dinner in the boat most days if you keep the boat moving with the current and stay on the drift lines where the bottom transitions from sand to broken shell.

Porgies have been thick around any structure holding bait — the rockpiles off New Harbor and the drop-offs near the Coast Guard station have been loaded, and if you've got kids aboard or just want steady bend in the rod, sandworms on a simple high-low rig will keep everyone busy between the bigger fish efforts.

Now, the question everyone's been asking me at the dock — where are the bonito and albies? We flagged this water as one of the top zones on the coastwide watch list, and I stand by that read. The temperature break I felt this week is exactly the kind of setup that pulls albies and bonito up onto the rips once the bait gets pushed and concentrated by the building current. We're not there yet — nobody's boated one off the island as of this week, and I don't want to tell you different. But the ingredients are on the table: warm water offshore, a cold edge developing right where we fish, and the tide building back toward the August new moon. If I were rigging up for it, I'd have a 7-weight or a light spin rod with small Deadly Dicks and Epoxy Jigs ready to go, and I'd be watching the North Rip and the water off Southeast Light closely on calm mornings — that's usually where the first scout shows up around here.

Looking ahead, expect the bass to stay locked into that dawn, dusk, and full-dark program as long as the surface stays warm, so plan your trips around the tide changes rather than the clock. Bluefish should keep providing the daytime entertainment on bait schools, fluke will stay steady on the drift, and I'd keep that light tackle rigged in the rocket launcher just in case that first bonito shows up on the temperature break we're all watching for.
